entities.name: Stabat Mater
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
Stabat Mater, a poignant and theologically rich poem, is attributed to Jacopone da Todi, a 13th-century Italian Franciscan friar, and is believed to have been composed around 1280. This literary work emerged within the context of the medieval church's evolving relationship with the laity and the growing emphasis on personal piety and devotion. It holds immense significance in Christian liturgical traditions, particularly in the Catholic Church, where it is used in the context of the Feast of Our Lady of Sorrows. Stabat Mater encapsulates the profound sorrow Mary experienced during the crucifixion of Jesus, reflecting the human condition and suffering, key themes that resonate throughout the history of Christian thought.

The text, structured as a sequence of 20 stanzas, became integral to the liturgical practice of the church, especially during the Lent and Holy Week. Its impact was further amplified in the 17th century when composers such as Giovanni Battista Pergolesi set the text to music, creating a masterful oratorio that popularized the work across Europe. This adaptation brought Stabat Mater into the concert hall, bridging the gap between sacred and secular music, and ensuring its enduring legacy in Western music culture. The poem's emotional depth and vivid imagery have inspired countless artistic interpretations across various media, including paintings, sculptures, and operas.
